This review will be a little bit biased as I bought the game mostly out of nostalgia. 
It has to be over a decade ago now, somewhere around 2013-2014 that I happened upon the game after watching a livestream from the Yogscast. Had it stayed as such then I probably wouldn’t have ever played it but it just so happened that not much later I was hospitalised due to a severe bout of sickness, making me unable to leave bed. It didn’t take long browsing the internet to learn of this relatively obscure app from China called Tongbu. It provided apple users the means to download cracked versions of apps on the app store, for free without having to jailbreak your device. Which as a young, less scrupulous child that was never quite able to get cydia working meant that I could play games instead of staring at a dreary ceiling all day.

Anyhow, I believe I quickly played and then finished both sorcery 1 and 2, the third instalment not having been released yet. This brings us to today where, after remembering the games in a dream, I have once again played both, now with a more critical eye. 
First and foremost, the story is enjoyable if not very unique, there’s nothing there that besmirches the writing but it is a bit dated. The gamebooks which these games are based on are over 40 years old at this point so if you’re even a tepid reader or consumer of fantasy media there won’t be anything that is likely to impress you per se. That said, the game has a certain authenticity in its writing that I often find missing in modern media, maybe this is just a conjuration of my mind but nevertheless it is something that I appreciate. The occasional art work from John Blanche, whom was one of the principal artists and miniature painters for Games Workshop until his retirement back in 2023, also helps to bring the in-game world alive. 

If you just want to play a story game then you will likely be satisfied with this series.

That said, nothing is perfect and this series certainly is not either. On a technical level there are occasionally issues with text appearing warped, this seems to be common enough that I have found steam forum threads on the matter and it might be fixed with a reinstallation. It didn’t overly bother me as it only happens occasionally but it is an issue. As for the story, I will not spoil anything. A particular mechanic in sorcery 2 bothered me a little bit in how it makes you backtrack through the game but that's just a minor annoyance that was likely meant for the player to experience more of what the game has to offer. 

I do not know if the cloud saves for this game still work, I imagine that they will but regardless I don’t know if the game should be pinging, what my firewall is saying are google analytics servers, on game open. This may be a miscategorisation and as I have not checked myself I’m not passing any strict judgement on that front. That said I must give kudos to the Inkle team for publishing their scripting language for this game. You can find it on github alongside documentation on how to use it.

I believe that’s all I have to say, I enjoyed my time playing these two instalments and will likely continue on with the next two as well. Goodbye.

First game was really good and I enjoyed it, but the second one.. I dunno.. at the end of Sorcery 2 you can be sent back in time if you didn’t get all the clues to open the gate, which is likely to happen since one wrong decision can keep you from getting all of them.

But being sent back in time means you have to replay all the previous stuff. I happened to miss just one clue because I chose the wrong alley once and didn’t encounter the event that gives you the clue. Apart from that I was really satisfied with the playthrough and my decisions. But now I would have to redo everything except for that one choice, probably 1-2h of gameplay.

Alternatively, you can finish the game without all the clues, but then you get the "bad" ending and become cursed, which negatively affects your character in the later games.

Ironically, this is exactly the reason why I also dropped the game a few years ago and never continued with Sorcery 3. Now the exact same thing has happened again and I’m wondering if I should just bin this game for real.

It just feels kind of frustrating that a single wrong turn can immediately lock you out of the "best" ending only for the player to realize it hours later.

Game is marketed as a Choose Your Own Adventure experience that routinely invalidates it's own premise by railroading player choice into one static binary result, often leading to complete dead-ends, unfair situations and the illusion of choice. Of thousands of choices in a game predicated upon choice, there is only one right way to play. This makes the game virtually indistinguisable from a standard visual novel with extra steps and is unfun to boot.

Play if you enjoy reading a story. Avoid if you want to roleplay or actually have the choices you make in a CYOA game respected. Requiring meta-knowledge of specific decision trees well in advance of other branching paths just to proceed with the story in the way you initially chose is poor design completely antithetical to the genre this game (and I'm assuming the other 3 parts) are predicated upon.

It's a fun game for the most part. The story-telling and characters are good enough that you'll likely be immersed and entertained. As for the choice aspect, it's a bit of a hit and miss. Surviving/progressing through certain parts is sometimes down to pure luck when picking your way through a sequence of options the game provides you with. I feel like there could've been a lot more creativity here, like giving clues as to what the right option might be, for example. It gets annoying (borderline frustrating) when you end up dying the same way to different sequences of choices, so you'll likely end up speeding your way through every option until you get the right one. That doesn't exactly make for good gameplay, and it can quickly ruin your immersion in the story. It's a significant flaw in the game's design, but luckily one that only occurs once every so often.

I bought Warlock of Firetop Mountain on my Nintendo Switch, and, while I liked the art and gameplay, I did not like the abusiveness of the game. There was no back-tracking allowed even when it was logical to be able to do so. There were many "you chose poorly, you die/lose everything/etc" choices without enough foreshadowing to help make better choices. On and on. Basically felt like an abusive DM/GM was running a game just to abuse the player.

I thought maybe the Sorcery! games would be a bit different, but, no. It still has that signature Steve Jackson abusive GM/DM feel to it.

Every encounter in Sorcery! is basically "don't trust this person, but don't hurt them either!" B/c if you trust them they'll shaft you. But, if you hurt them, they'll also shaft you. So, often, the only seemingly "good" choice is to just bypass the encounters.

However, this game tracks sleep and eating. So, if you bypass too much stuff, you'll be a starving, low-hp character i no time. Since you won't have any encounters to get food or enough money to buy food.

And money is very hard to come by in his game. One town wanted 3 gold to get room and board. Cool, I finally get 3 gold. But, no back-tracking (rolls-eyes), so push on to the next town. This place was 5 gold. Well, ****. I only have 3 gold, man!

Everything in the game feels like it's designed to punish and frustrate you instead of feeling like the risk was worth a reward.

There's a tough monster fighting you for seemingly no reason. Ok, kill it. Do you get anything for your trouble? Often, no. So, it feels pointless. But, many times you're railroaded into the combat.

And the combat itself is aggravating. You and your opponent choose how much overall strangth to use, from holding a defense, to a light jab to full on charge attack, each taking more and more energy. Each enemy has different cadences to attack, defend, etc. But, if you defend while it attacks you still get -1 damage. If you attack and it has a higher score, you get hurt but it doesn't. Lot of combats turn into menial slug fests where you're gonna get damaged by just DEFENDIGN yourself.

I guess I'm just not a fan of the true-to-book translation these games had, b/c it just brought all the nasty parts of 80's Fighting Fantasy style garbage over to a computer version.

Sorcery! Is forty-three years old overall as of this review and this version is nine years old. When I first played this version made by Inkle, I didn’t expect it to be anywhere as good as it is. When I played through even just Part 1 and Part 2, I realized just why the original gamebooks were so popular. It still stands, though admittedly Inkle did do a bit of updating to the story in 2016. One of my favourite game series of all time! 

— A good fantasy story bettered by the fact that it’s reactive and often dark and/or humorous. 
— You won’t see everything every playthrough and it can get /rough/ at times.
— There’s many niche reactions that are built upon the path of choices behind you across the games, some things being profoundly hard to see without a guide.
— Has a mechanic which encourages you to retry choices and see them again. So, don’t feel bad about save scumming — after all, people playing gamebooks definitely “cheated” too!
— The combat is simple and may seem arcane, but reading the text will help. It can feel obscured but there’s a strategy to it that can make fights way faster. And gear/magic can be very helpful. 

 Sorcery! Part 1 and Part 2 reviews often says it “feels like playing a singleplayer DnD game” but I’ve played many interactive fiction games and I can say “it feels like a damn good interactive fantasy fiction game” instead. It doesn’t have the same character building as DnD and the fantasy world is removed from comparisons to the modern DnD setting for the most part. Will it satisfy the itch for a tabletop campaign? Maybe, but I feel so-so about that common comparison. It has a unique magic system that will make you excited for items that you probably wouldn’t be excited for any other RPG. The art is scant but great and the writing doesn’t try to overstay its welcome. 

— Note that this is a mobile port.
—  I’m not sure if they’ve changed it since I played it last but the audio cannot be adjusted in game, so you’d have to limit the audio using your system.
— There’s no flashing images. Images are still.
— I always had a problem with how light the text is, if it were a little bit darker, it would be better to read.  
— The game would be served well by having a journal of sorts for those who have memory issues. Part Two is a lot longer than Part One. Taking long breaks may feel punishing and have you lost and confused.
— There’s some issues where it feels like the game doesn’t remember what you did, and some grammar issues, but there isn’t very many of both thankfully. 
— The art can sometimes be hard to parse. I /like/ this about this art style, though.
